findings.evidence: Rank the survivors by the user's stated priorities; default order is spelling reliability, then memorability, then descriptiveness, then TLD fit.
findings.fix: Shorten step 3 to the part the model would not do unprompted: 'Default ranking: spelling reliability first; when the top pick wins one axis and loses another (for example memorable but needs a premium .com), state the trade-off in one line.' Drop the generic restatement of ranking by user priorities.

findings.evidence: "Suggest names for a sustainable clothing store and explain the brand fit." labeled should_trigger false, while the description says to trigger 'even if the user only describes the business'
findings.fix: Make the negative an unambiguous near-miss, for example 'Suggest names for a sustainable clothing line's spring collection; we already own our domain and don't need a new one.', or relabel this query should_trigger true

findings.evidence: No eval covers step 4 (first choice taken: another TLD vs modifier vs new name)
findings.fix: Add an eval such as 'rosiescrumb.com is taken by a bakery in Ohio; we're a bakery in Leeds. What should we do?' with assertions: picks exactly one path, recommends a new name or a clearly distinct option because the holder is in the same category, and states that path's cost

findings.evidence: WHOIS fallback ... then `whois -h <server> <name>` (label rule at line 26: 'its WHOIS said "not found"')
findings.fix: Add a WHOIS classification rule: 'Registry WHOIS phrasing varies (for example .de returns "Status: free", others "No match" or "NOT FOUND"). Map an explicit no-record reply to `not found in registry`, a record with a creation date to `registered`, and anything else, including restricted or rate-limit text, to `unverified`.'

findings.evidence: “Ideation is cheap; the skill's value is screening names hard and never presenting a guess as a lookup.” This introductory declaration repeats the operational rules below rather than adding knowledge.
findings.fix: Remove the introductory paragraph and begin with Defaults; retain the concrete screening rules, lookup distinctions and gotchas.

findings.evidence: “Suggest names for a sustainable clothing store and explain the brand fit.” is labeled false, while “Give me brandable names for a secure family photo-sharing product.” at line 27 is labeled true. Both request brand names without mentioning domains, leaving the intended implicit-domain boundary inconsistent.
findings.fix: Keep the implicit-business positive and rewrite the clothing-store negative to explicitly exclude domains, for example: “Suggest names for a sustainable clothing store and explain the brand fit; do not suggest domains.”

findings.evidence: “Same name, another TLD: when the audience types the name more than it searches for it on `.com`”. Following this branch for a direct-navigation-heavy audience selects the option most exposed to the acknowledged .com traffic and email leakage.
findings.fix: Prefer another TLD when discovery is mainly through search or links, users can reliably retain the full address, and the .com holder is unrelated. Prefer a new name when users habitually type the bare .com or significant email confusion is expected; retain the explicit leakage warning.

findings.evidence: The prescribed command is “curl -sS -L -o rdap.json -w '%{http_code} %{url_effective}' https://rdap.org/domain/<name>”, without a connection or total deadline, although line 35 provides a timeout fallback. A server that accepts a connection and then stalls can prevent that fallback from being reached promptly.
findings.fix: Add explicit limits such as --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 to curl, and bound WHOIS execution with a tool deadline as well. Route expired lookups to unverified without retrying.
